en: Kaiser Library 138 = NGMPP C 14/15:
*Devamanuṣyamantra-Avalokiteśvarastotra-ṭīkā*, as mentioned by Tucci in *Animadversiones*.
% Text published by Minaev; = Tib. Tōh. 2726 % also see NGMPP A 1311-22(3) *Carpaṭipādastotra* % another work by this author: A 936-11(8) *Mantrasādhanāṅga*

[Cover Page: O Venerable One, regarding the *stotra* (hymn) of Avalokiteśvara for gods and humans, what is the *carapatipāda* (the sequence of verses), O Venerable One, for the purpose of recitation? What is the *stotra-koṭikā* (the ten-million-fold hymn)?
[1v] Homage to Lokeśvara!
Having bowed to the Guru, the Lord of the World, the protector of all the worlds, who is the supreme non-dual form inseparable from compassion and emptiness;
This commentary on the *Carpaṭistuti* was composed by me, Śrī Śīlasāgara, at the instigation of the illustrious Meghamahāpātra.
Who is Meghamahāpātra? [I] cannot identify him.
Note: Śīlasāgara is known as Vanaratna’s teacher;
neither of these names is mentioned by Tucci.

"O God," and so forth. O God, whose feet are bowed to by gods, humans, and asuras; O you who have overcome birth, old age, sickness, and death; O Lord of the World, protect—meaning, preserve—me, who am without refuge and devoid of a protector. This is the first connection [of the words]. O compassionate one, O merciful one, "you should exercise compassion"—that is, the state of pity—this is the second connection.

Gods, humans, and asuras—these are the "devamanuṣyāsurās. He whose feet are bowed down by them is "devamanuṣyāsuranatacaraṇa"; the address to him is "O devamanuṣyāsuranatacaraṇa. By this, it is indicated that the Blessed One is the Teacher among gods and humans. Birth, old age, sickness, and death—these constitute "janmajarārujamaraṇa."

"O you by whom birth, old age, sickness, and death have been struck down and eliminated—O you who have overcome birth, old age, sickness, and death! With this, the Blessed One’s perfection of abandonment (*prahāṇasaṃpad*) is proclaimed. "O Lord of the World (*lokeśa*), turn toward [me]! With this, the Blessed One’s perfection of attainment (*prāptisaṃpad*) is manifested. By the word "protect" (*rakṣa*), the perfection of the welfare of others (*parārthasaṃpad*) is stated.
By the phrase "exercise compassion," the perfection of compassion (*karuṇāsaṃpad*) is revealed. (1)

"Saṃsāra... and so forth. The connection is: "O Greatly Compassionate One, O Greatly Merciful One, do not disregard me. How am I? Immersed in the midst of the ocean of *saṃsāra*. Again, how am I? Shattered by being struck by the great waves of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Again, how am I? Crying out. "O Greatly Compassionate One, protect me"—this is the second connection. "I bow to you, sir"—this is the third connection. "Do not disregard me; do not treat me with contempt."

Samsara itself is an ocean; its center is where I am submerged and cast down. It is filled with the great waves of the afflictions (*kleśa*), by which I have been completely overwhelmed and shattered. Crying out and weeping—protect me, who am thus distinguished, and guard me! I bow to you, the Lord of the World (*lokeśa*); the meaning is that I pay homage to you with the intention of seeking refuge. (2)

"Thirst," and so forth. O Blessed One, O possessor of qualities such as sovereignty! Protect me; guard me. Not only protect me, but look upon me—behold me. Of what nature am I? One whose eyes are afflicted by the darkness of thirst (*tṛṣṇā-timira*). Furthermore, of what nature am I? One whose body is overwhelmed by the great terror of death. The connection is: "until I go to the uneven Avīci hell. Thirst itself is the darkness (*timira*), the gloom; one whose eyes, that is, whose vision, are afflicted—that is, agitated—by that is meant.

"O Blessed One, O Vanquisher of Māra, protect—meaning guard—me who am of such a nature, whose body and limbs are overwhelmed and constrained by death itself, which is the greatest terror. Look upon me! The word *yāvat* indicates a limit; it is indicated that this is the occasion for protection only so long as I do not go—that is, until I reach—the uneven, dreadful Avīci hell. (3)

O Lord, your compassion is as vast as space; like the torrents of water from a cloud, it flows incessantly and without end across all lands—high and low, dry and wet—reaching every place without exception. (24)

"O Protector," and so forth. O Protector, just as a stream of water flows incessantly and without interruption across all lands—whether on dry ground, in water, or over high and low terrain—so too does your compassion, vast as the sky, flow toward sentient beings; such is the connection of the words. O Protector, O Lord of the World! "Compassion" means *karuṇā*; it is yours, O Lord of the World, vast and expansive like the sky, directed toward sentient beings, that is, living creatures. "Ambuda" means a cloud; its "water" is the rain, and its "stream" is the downpour.

It is "vast" (*bahu*) and it is "land" (*deśa*), "dry ground" (*sthala*), "water" (*jala*), "low-lying" (*nimna*), and "elevated" (*unnata*); thus, it is "land, water, low-lying, and elevated" (*sthalajalanimnonnata*). It is both that [terrain] and a "vast land" (*bahudeśa*), and so it is "in that [vast land consisting of land, water, low-lying, and elevated terrain]. He "moves" (*sarati*) or "goes" (*gacchati"). "Continuously" (*nirantaram*) means as there is no interval (*antarāla*). "Unceasingly" (*aniśam*) means day and night (*rātrindivam*). "Without remainder" (*aśeṣe*) means that for which no remainder exists; thus, it is "in that [which is without remainder]. (24)
By whatever merit I have gained from this remembrance of the Blessed One, may this world, unimpaired, attain residence upon the mountain of Potalaka and produce various beautiful delights. 25.

"Thus," and so forth. By this recollection of the Blessed One, whatever merit I possess, by that may this world become unimpaired; may it obtain residence on the glorious Mount Potalaka—indeed, may it obtain residence on the glorious Mount Potalaka itself—and may it produce beautiful and manifold delights: such is the connection [of the words].

Thus, by means of the twenty-four verses just mentioned, there is the recollection of the Blessed One, which is *bhagavat-smaraṇa*. Whatever merit (*puṇya*) or virtue (*kuśala*) exists therein—by that virtue, may this world (*jagat*), this universe, attain its dwelling and stability upon that very mountain known as Śrī Potalaka, so that it may be unimpaired and fruitful (*akṣuṇṇa*); and may they obtain manifold delights (*vividhavilāsa*).
"He is both beautiful and possessed of manifold charms; thus, 'sundaravividhavilāsa'—may he generate or produce that. || 25 ||
